name: Priya Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and play viola in a small chamber orchestra, record practice passages and teach four private pupils. I have a music degree and twenty years of paid playing, but carrying a viola case between a school hall and a late train still wears me out. I love hearing a pupil finally find the note without my hand on the bow.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are the household bills fitting around the music?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner repairs bicycles, our children are grown, and we pay a mortgage. We have three weeks of bills saved, my own fees are below the usual rate, and there are few similar chairs nearby. I use AI occasionally to draft a concert notice, then check every date and name myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the orchestra that quicker concert notices are fine if players still see the fee and rehearsal time in writing. I would ask the organiser to name every paid rehearsal before we print the poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even without big AI changes, one cancelled school concert can make the mortgage week tight. Three weeks saved is too little for me to call the calendar secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This November I would keep my four pupils and the paid orchestra chair, and ask for signed rehearsal and cancellation terms for winter. In the plateau’s first year I would request an actual pension estimate, then compare the figure with our bills before choosing any retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the next gap between paid concerts, even in this quiet picture. My viola does not pay the mortgage while it sits in its case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which term matters most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cancellation fee matters when a hall changes its date after I have turned down another job. I would want that number written beside the rehearsal fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would an estimate mean stopping work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have no retirement date set. An estimate tells us what might be there; the booked music still pays today.

say: I would ask for **written rehearsal fees** before a concert poster goes out.
I would welcome **quicker notices** if player hours stay visible.
think: A **cancelled concert** could make the mortgage week tight.
Our **three-week reserve** does not cover a long booking gap.
do: Keep **four pupils** and the paid orchestra chair through winter.
Request **signed rehearsal terms** and cancellation fees before accepting dates.
Request an **actual pension estimate** in the plateau’s first year and compare it with bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about existing gaps in paid music.
S0.quote: My viola does not pay the mortgage while it sits in its case.
fieldNote: Her **thin reserve** and low fees make even a plateau financially tense.
She will check an **actual pension estimate** without assuming a pension or choosing a retirement date.

Request signed rehearsal and cancellation fees before accepting concert dates
Request actual pension estimate in first plateau year; compare figure with bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the hall that generated practice tracks can help, but a beginner group still needs a paid viola teacher. I would ask whether eight families will pay for a safe Saturday class before promising one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two practice recordings I sell each month may shrink to none. Those fees buy groceries, and I cannot use our three-week reserve to pay a room or another teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would get a written room hire and price a six-week beginner viola group with an experienced bow teacher paid to watch the children. In disruption’s first year, if both monthly recording sales disappear, I would open only after eight families prepay enough for my teaching and preparation, the bow teacher’s wage, room, safe instrument hire and train fares; if a viola is unsafe, I would replace it or defer and refund the whole group below eight safe paid places, and renew only on that same full floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because those two recordings could stop paying. A full viola class is not a wage until every cost and both teachers are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you take a family’s money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after the hall signs the room and hire charge. A promised room is not a place to teach eight children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if one hired viola is damaged before class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would get a safe replacement before playing. If I cannot keep eight safe paid places, I would defer and refund the entire group rather than run it below cost.

I would ask for a **paid teacher** to supervise young players.
think: Two monthly **recording sales** may vanish, removing grocery money from my lower-paid music work.

do: Start **Saturday viola class** after both monthly recordings end, written room/hire before deposits and eight fees covering room/own teaching/preparation/supervisor/safe instruments/trains.
Replace **unsafe violas** or defer and refund whole group below eight safe paid places.
Renew **Saturday class** only if eight safe fees cover teaching, preparation, supervisor, room, instruments and trains.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing practice-recording fees.

fieldNote: The **eight-place floor** covers her teaching and preparation, paid bow supervision, room, safe hire and trains.
An **unsafe viola** means safe replacement or whole-group deferral and refund when the floor fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the orchestra that thinking AGI in 2028 can undercut recorded practice parts before robot players arrive around 2031. I would ask for written live rehearsal dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect both monthly recording sales to end in 2028 and one school rehearsal contract may be cut too. That would remove a serious piece of my lower pay while the mortgage and train fares keep coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would request signed live dates and total the recording and rehearsal fees that might go. In the first year after 2028, if the recordings end and paid rehearsal hours fall, I would apply only to a posted paid school music coordinator vacancy accepting my music degree and teaching record, with written net pay after travel replacing the lost fees and a last train that fits; I would keep the orchestra and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the expected recording losses; losing a school contract too would alarm me. I have been awake making the mortgage sums already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your degree guarantee that school job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The school’s actual posting must accept my music degree and classroom experience. Few local posts appear, and I will not leave paid music for a possibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do robot players change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card puts hands-on robots around 2031, three years after thinking AGI. The first threat to my pay is the recording price in 2028.

I would explain **2028 AGI** could affect recordings before robot players in 2031.
think: I expect **two recording sales** to end and worry a school contract could follow.
My **mortgage week** has little room for a large fee gap.
do: Request **signed live dates** and total exposed recording and rehearsal fees now.
Apply for **posted school coordinator** after recording and rehearsal losses only if degree and teaching qualify; require written replacement net after travel.
Keep **orchestra and pupils** until a signed offer and workable last train.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected recording losses; an additional school cut would alarm me.
S2.quote: I have been awake making the mortgage sums already.
fieldNote: The **2028 recording loss** is expected, while school-hour loss is a further condition for her job application.
A **school vacancy** must accept her music degree and teaching record and replace lost net pay after travel.

steps.text: Request signed rehearsal dates and total exposed recording fees this month
Apply after recording/rehearsal losses to posted school role accepting degree/teaching; written replacement net after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell pupils that AGI by 2031 reaches scores and bookings before a robot could hold a viola around 2034. I would check a new score tool by ear, not sell it as a teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect practice-track sales to slide over five years, and the school may buy fewer rehearsal days. Five years gives me time to ask for another paid term, but it does not create local vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the school for a written paid teaching and preparation term. If the school funds instruction on its score checker and approves local storage, I would test only my own nameless passage, play it against the printed score and stop at a wrong note or any file leaving the school; in the first year after 2031 I would keep paid pupils and school work only while the fees still arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing recordings even with five years to prepare. I can check a score myself, but I cannot make a school renew its paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put a pupil’s recording into the checker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a pupil’s name and playing stay in the school folder. My own nameless passage is enough to see whether the tool follows the printed notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the school offers unpaid preparation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for paid preparation in writing before taking another term. Practice outside the room is still part of my work.

think: I expect **practice-track sales** to slide before 2031.

feel: I feel **anxious** about likely recording decline.
S3.quote: I can check a score myself, but I cannot make a school renew its paid hours.
fieldNote: A **new score tool** needs funded instruction, approved storage, owned nameless material and manual playing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the orchestra that a decade until 2036 is time to put player and teaching fees on paper. Robot viola players around 2039 are a later question than paid rehearsal dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may want fewer late trains, but we cannot plan retirement from an amount I have never checked. Recordings may be gone by 2036, and our tiny reserve still makes a cancelled term matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request an actual pension estimate and signed teaching hours, then save one tenth of any extra cleared concert fee after mortgage, food and train fares toward two months of bills. Over the decade I would start the Saturday class only after written room hire and eight safe paid places cover my teaching and preparation, bow supervision, room, instruments and travel. In the first year after 2036 I would renew on that same floor while keeping paid pupils and live chairs; I would replace unsafe instruments or defer and refund the whole group below eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the thin reserve and later recording income, even with a decade. A calendar can be long and the paid line can still be short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no extra concert fees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I save nothing new from that source. I will not describe a two-month target as money already in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop playing when the estimate comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I would compare the actual figure with our bills and my health. We have no retirement date agreed.

say: I would demand **written player fees** over the decade.
I would distinguish **2036 AGI** from robot viola players around 2039.
think: An **unknown pension amount** cannot pay our present mortgage.
Later **recording loss** and a thin reserve still matter.
do: Request **actual pension estimate** and signed teaching hours; keep paid pupils/live chairs during the class test.
Save one tenth of **extra cleared concert fees** after essentials toward two months of bills.
Start **Saturday class** with written room, eight safe fees covering room/teaching/preparation/supervisor/instruments/trains; renew after 2036 on same floor or defer/refund everyone.
feel: I feel **anxious** about real income risk despite the longer timetable.
S4.quote: A calendar can be long and the paid line can still be short.
fieldNote: Her **two-month target** depends on extra paid concert fees after mortgage, food and travel.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because recorded parts could vanish before I can replace those fees, and a lost school day would make the mortgage sums worse. Written paid dates, an actual school vacancy that accepts my degree and a net offer after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a beginner class has a safe viola for every paid child. The hire and the teacher’s preparation are real bills, even when the lesson looks cheerful.

headlineQuote: The hire and the teacher’s preparation are real bills, even when the lesson looks cheerful.
portrait: Priya is a **58-year-old viola player** with a music degree, four pupils and long experience.
Her **lower fees**, three-week reserve, mortgage and few nearby chairs make booking gaps serious.
She uses **AI occasionally** and tests a score checker only after funded instruction, approved storage and manual playing.
Her **Saturday class** requires eight safe paid places covering both teachers, preparation, room, instruments and travel.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could erase recorded-part fees and cut school rehearsal pay before she replaces it.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **written paid dates**, an actual school vacancy accepting her degree and a replacement net offer after travel.
